Anakims
AN-uh-kims
n. pl.
Hebrew Anaqim, the descendants of Anak, whose name is connected with the word for a neck-chain or collar — the long-necked. They held Hebron and the hill country of Judah, and their reputation is what turned Israel back at Kadeshbarnea for forty years.

Biblical Definition

The Anakims are the giants of Hebron, and they are the measure by which every other tall people in Scripture is described — the Emims, the Zamzummims, and the Rephaim are all reckoned as the Anakims. The ten spies made them the whole substance of their report: there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight (Numbers 13:33). That last clause is the fatal one, since no spy could possibly know how he looked to a giant; the report had already passed from observation into imagination. Forty years later Moses names the fear honestly and answers it: A people great and tall, the children of the Anakims, whom thou knowest, and of whom thou hast heard say, Who can stand before the children of Anak! (Deuteronomy 9:2) — and then, Understand therefore this day, that the LORD thy God is he which goeth over before thee. Caleb, at eighty-five, asked for the very mountain the spies had feared: thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there… if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out (Joshua 14:12). He drove them out. There was none of the Anakims left in the land of the children of Israel: only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod, there remained (Joshua 11:22) — and Gath afterward produced Goliath.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 has no ANAKIM entry. The Hebrew plural is retained by the King James translators, as with Emims and Rephaims; the root is generally connected with a neck-chain, hence the traditional gloss long-necked.

expand to see more

ANAKIMS, n. pl. — The descendants of Anak; a race of tall men who inhabited Hebron and the hill country of southern Canaan.

The name is usually derived from Hebrew anaq, a necklace or collar, whence the sense of long-necked or of those who wore the ornaments of chiefs.

Arba, from whom Hebron was formerly called Kirjatharba, was a great man among the Anakims (Joshua 14:15).

Three sons of Anak are named at Numbers 13:22 — Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai — and Caleb drove out all three (Joshua 15:14).

The survivors at Gaza, Gath, and Ashdod (Joshua 11:22) supply the background to Goliath of Gath and his brethren.

Key Scripture

Numbers 13:33 — "And there we saw the giants, the sons of Anak, which come of the giants: and we were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight."

Deuteronomy 9:2 — "A people great and tall, the children of the Anakims, whom thou knowest, and of whom thou hast heard say, Who can stand before the children of Anak!"

Joshua 11:22 — "There was none of the Anakims left in the land of the children of Israel: only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod, there remained."

Joshua 14:12 — "Now therefore give me this mountain, whereof the LORD spake in that day; for thou heardest in that day how the Anakims were there, and that the cities were great and fenced: if so be the LORD will be with me, then I shall be able to drive them out, as the LORD said."

Joshua 14:15 — "And the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba; which Arba was a great man among the Anakims. And the land had rest from war."

Modern Corruption

Numbers 13:33 has been made the proof text of Christian self-esteem teaching — the idea that Israel failed because they thought too little of themselves. The text says they failed because they thought too little of God, and the grasshopper line is the report’s clearest evidence of unbelief.

expand to see more

We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight. Preachers regularly treat the first clause as the sin and prescribe a higher self-image as the cure. Read the second clause: they claim to know how they appeared to the giants, which is information no spy possessed. Unbelief is not merely fearful; it is inventive, and it fills in the enemy’s opinion for him. The remedy Scripture actually gives is nowhere in the neighbourhood of self-image. Caleb and Joshua saw the same giants and the same walls and said, the LORD is with us: fear them not. Moses, rehearsing it forty years on, does not tell Israel they are stronger than they think; he tells them the LORD goeth over before them as a consuming fire. The size of the Anakim was never in dispute. The size of God was.

The second thing to mark is Caleb’s request. At eighty-five he asked for Hebron specifically because the Anakim were there and the cities were great and fenced, and he hedged it with the humblest possible clause — if so be the LORD will be with me. That is not bravado; it is faith that names the difficulty accurately and then names God accurately. The generation that refused the mountain died in the wilderness; the man who asked for it at eighty-five got it, and the land had rest from war. Forty-five years of waiting on a promise did not diminish him, because he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Anaq (H6061), Anak, and Anaqim (H6062), the Anakims; connected with anaq (H6059), to encircle the neck, hence a necklace or collar.

expand to see more

Hebrew Anaq (H6061) — Anak; the man from whom the clan is named (Numbers 13:22).

Hebrew Anaqim (H6062) — the Anakims; Deuteronomy 2:10-11, 9:2, Joshua 11:21-22.

Hebrew anaq (H6059) — to put about the neck, to adorn with a chain; the likely root of the name.

Hebrew Nephilim (H5303) — giants; the word rendered giants in Numbers 13:33 and Genesis 6:4.

Hebrew Qiryath Arba — Kirjatharba, the city of Arba, Hebron’s older name (Joshua 14:15).

Usage

"We were in our own sight as grasshoppers (Numbers 13:33) — the report that cost a generation the land."

"Who can stand before the children of Anak! (Deuteronomy 9:2) — Moses quoting the fear back before answering it."

"Now therefore give me this mountain (Joshua 14:12) — Caleb asking at eighty-five for the giants’ country."
